p.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics: The Role of Timing and Network Heterogeneity
p.venue: Not visible in snippet (preprint or journal, 2025)

ext.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics
ext.year: Not printed in the text (metadata hint says 2025; latest cited reference is 2024, Palermo et al.)
ext.venue: Preprint submitted to Elsevier (29 pages). No journal named in the text. Affiliations: Xiamen University of Technology (Cai); University of Southampton (Gerding, Brede).
ext.document_type: Preprint manuscript (simulation and mean-field analysis; not empirical)
ext.coverage: Read all 2506 lines of the text file in three chunks (lines 1-955, 956-1755, 1756-2506), covering abstract, introduction, Sections 2-5, Appendices A-E, acknowledgements and references. Nothing omitted. Paul markup: none supplied (the task listed no markup files), so paul_markup is empty. Coverage is complete for the text as extracted; figure content is read only from axis labels and captions.
ext.research_question: How do the timing and distribution of a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign shape the final vote share in a voter model, and how does network degree heterogeneity change the optimal campaign timing? Two settings: (1) one controller (A) against a constant, fixed opponent (B); (2) two controllers choosing start times simultaneously in a zero-sum game (paper Sections 1, 2, abstract p.1).
ext.theory: Non-progressive voter model (reversible opinion changes; Masuda 2015) with heterogeneous mean-field theory and relaxation-time analysis (Son et al. 2008). Degree heterogeneity drives timescales. Competitive timing and budget allocation are analysed with interior-point optimization, stochastic hill climbing, and minimax-based iterative search for Nash equilibria in a zero-sum game. Partial zealotry (Masuda et al. 2010; Moreno et al. 2020) adds agent heterogeneity. Authors contrast their smooth zealotry with latency models (Palermo et al. 2024).
ext.data:
Simulated and real networks, no empirical opinion or vote-outcome data.
(a) Synthetic configuration-model scale-free networks. Main experiments: N = 10^4 nodes, target mean degree 10 (realized 10.5), degree exponent lambda in [1.6, 5], k_max = sqrt(N) (p.11, p.25). Individual-optimization experiments: N = 10^2, mean degree 6, k_max = 30, 10 realizations (p.17, p.25). Complete-network zealotry experiment: N = 10^2 (p.26). Each figure reports 100 or 10 realizations (see captions).
(b) Real networks, Table 1 (p.11): Congress votes N=219, 764 edges, mean degree 7.0, lambda about 1.9 (text: mentions between US politicians with supportive or opposing edges). Facebook N=3862, 87324 edges, mean degree 45.2, lambda about 1.6 (users affiliated with one corporation). Advogato N=6541, 51127 edges, mean degree 15.6, lambda about 1.7 (trust network). Wikipedia Elections N=7118, 103689 edges, mean degree 29.1, lambda about 1.5 (positive/negative votes between users; these are Wikipedia admin-style votes, not political elections). Twitter N=22322, 31823 edges, mean degree 2.9, lambda about 4.3 (following network).
Unit of analysis: individual node (agent). Time: simulated horizons T=16 (short) and T=256 (long), dimensionless model time, not calendar periods. Initial opinion share 0.5 for all nodes (or 0 in some experiments, p.18, p.26); one illustrative example uses S_A(0)=0.55 with N=10^4, T=30 (p.5).
ext.method:
Analytical plus numerical simulation.
- Model (Eq. 1, p.4): each node's opinion-A probability x_i(t) evolves under neighbour influence and two controllers with time-varying gains a_i(t), b_i(t). Budget constraints sum of integrals <= b_A, b_B (p.3-4). Vote share S_A(T) = mean of x_i(T) (Eq. 2).
- Constant-opponent, uniform start (Sec 2.1, Eq. 3-5): A's gain is 0 until t_a, then b_A/((T-t_a)N); B's gain is constant b_B/(TN). Optimal t_a solved by interior-point method (p.5).
- Individual optimization (Sec 2.2, Eq. 6-7): each node has its own start time and budget; stochastic hill climbing (Algorithm 1, p.7), with L_max = N^2 iterations (p.26). Budget moves between nodes keep the total fixed.
- Heterogeneity extension (Sec 2.2.1, Eq. 8): partial zealots with probability q_i of resisting adoption of A when holding B.
- Game (Sec 2.3, Eq. 9; Algorithm 2, p.8): simultaneous choice of start times t_a, t_b; iterative alternating best responses (A maximizes, B minimizes S_A(T)) with step size mu = 1/i, stopping threshold 1e-9 (p.8).
- Mean-field (Sec 3, Eq. 10-11, derived in App. B): nodes grouped by degree k; closed-form x_k(t) and S_A(t).
- Relaxation times (Eq. 12-14, 19): normalized order parameter r_k(t); tau_relax,k and tau_relax as degree-weighted averages; l-percentage relaxation time tau^l.
- Taylor expansion (Eq. 15-18) to second order in 1/k, assuming (a_k+b_k)/k << 1.
- Numerical integration: 4th-order Runge-Kutta, time step 0.01 (p.11).
- Real-network experiments: Table 2 compares optimized t_a with t_a=0 at T in {16, 256} and b_A/b_B in {0.1, 1, 10}.
- Appendix A: single-node case with fully flexible allocation via calculus of variations (Eq. 20-30), yielding a transcendental equation for start time.
ext.identification: None in a causal sense; model-based simulation. Mean-field and Taylor predictions are validated against Runge-Kutta integration (Fig. 2, 3, 4c-f; p.11-16). Optimality of the start time is checked by a convex vote-share peak (Fig. 4c-d, p.15-16). Within-model comparison is optimized start versus t_a=0 (Table 2, p.18).
ext.scope: Population: abstract simulated networks (configuration model) and five public network datasets; no sampled human population. Era: none stated. Opinions: binary (A or B), simple contagion, unit link weights, complete knowledge of network topology assumed (p.22-23). Applications named as motivation only (marketing, politics, public health; p.1-2, p.22); no application-specific calibration or validation is reported.

key_findings.finding: Constant-opponent, uniform start: optimal strategy is to delay. The controller lets the opponent dominate early, reserves budget, and then increases allocation sharply near the deadline.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, p.16-17; Fig. 5a; Sec 1 p.3 (main finding i)
key_findings.numbers: Example budgets: N=10^4, T=30, b_A=1.5e4, b_B=1.2e4; S_A(0)=0.55 (p.5). Optimal control time (T - t_a) plotted for T in {1,...,512} (Fig. 5a).

key_findings.finding: Network heterogeneity shifts optimal timing with horizon. For short horizons, highly heterogeneous networks (low lambda) should start later; for long horizons they should start earlier.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, p.16-17; Sec 1 p.3 (main finding i)
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative pattern from Fig. 5a (T=16 vs T=256 curves). Fig. 4e: at T=16 the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82 (p.16).

key_findings.finding: Relaxation time increases with node degree; higher-degree nodes equilibrate more slowly. Mean-field and Taylor estimates track Runge-Kutta.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 2(a) relaxation time on a y-axis of about 52-56 across degree 2-92 (N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, lambda=1.6, 100 realizations). Uniform targeting: tau_relax,k approximately independent of initial state (p.10).

key_findings.finding: More heterogeneous networks (lower lambda) have longer overall equilibration times, driven by high-degree nodes.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 2(b) x-axis lambda in [1.6, 5]; y-axis tau_relax about 6.35-6.45. Text: more heterogeneous networks have longer timescales (quoted).

key_findings.finding: Degree of equilibrium l reverses the ranking of relaxation times. At low l, less heterogeneous networks (high lambda) take longer; near equilibrium, more heterogeneous networks take longer. Early changes are driven by low-degree nodes; late changes by high-degree nodes.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 3 uses N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, lambda=1.6 and 5, 100 realizations. Low/high degree split at 80%/20% (Pareto). Fig. 3(a) tau^l axis about 1-6 (inset 5-6.5 near equilibrium).

key_findings.finding: Real networks: optimized start time beats t_a=0 in every dataset, both horizons, and all budget ratios tested.
key_findings.numbers: Congress votes T=16: b_A/b_B=1 gives opt t_a 12.533, S_A 0.705 vs 0.500 at t_a=0; b_A/b_B=0.1 gives 14.730, 0.248 vs 0.117; b_A/b_B=10 gives 10.476, 0.958 vs 0.909. Twitter T=256, b_A/b_B=1: opt t_a 250.157, S_A 0.973 vs 0.500. Facebook T=16, b_A/b_B=10: 7.897, 0.907 vs 0.889.

key_findings.finding: Budget advantage means earlier start. A controller with more budget relative to its rival starts influence earlier; a disadvantaged controller starts later.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, Fig. 5b, p.17-18; Table 2; Appendix A Eq. 30, p.23-24
key_findings.numbers: Congress votes T=16: opt t_a falls from 14.730 (ratio 0.1) to 10.476 (ratio 10). Fig. 5b fixes T=16 with optimal start 9-15 across lambda and ratio 0.01-100 (axis).

key_findings.finding: Individual (node-specific) optimization improves vote share over a single uniform start, but absolute gains are small. Relative gains are largest for small budget ratios.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.2, Fig. 6(a)-(c), p.17-18; Appendix D p.26; Fig. 11(c) p.27
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 6(a) relative vote share S_indiv/S_const on axis 1.00-1.25 for b_A/b_B from 0.01 to 1 (N=100, mean degree 6, lambda=1.6, T=10, 10 realizations). Text: improvement very small in absolute numbers. Complete-network Fig. 11(c) relative axis 1.0-1.6.

key_findings.finding: Under node-specific optimization, small budgets target only low-degree nodes. Control gains fall with degree and start times rise with degree when the budget ratio is small; the pattern reverses for large ratios.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.2, Fig. 6(b)-(c), p.18; Appendix D Fig. 10(b)-(c), p.26
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 6(b) control gains axis 0-8; Fig. 6(c) starting times 4-10. Appendix D (b_A=b_B): positive correlation between budget and degree; inverse relation between degree and start time; about N^2 iterations for convergence (p.26).

key_findings.finding: Zealotry: 20% of nodes are partial zealots. Normal agents receive more resources than zealots at every q, and zealot allocations depend on q.
key_findings.numbers: Lowest zealotry q=0.1: max allocation to zealots under 20 vs near 25 for normal agents (p.19). For medium and large q, zealots receive fewer resources and later starts as degree rises. Normal agents: larger degree, larger budget, earlier start.

key_findings.finding: Complete-network zealotry (no degree structure, zealotry uniform on [0,1]): at large budget ratio, controller A starts earlier as zealotry rises up to a threshold near q=0.7, then reverses.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 11(a) control gains axis 0-250 for b_A/b_B in {0.1,...,100}; threshold q around 0.7 (text, p.27).

key_findings.finding: Game with two controllers: the controller with the larger budget starts first, and the second mover concentrates its budget in the final stage to pull back the vote share.
key_findings.numbers: N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, T=16, b_B=N*T, b_A=10*b_B, 100 realizations per Fig. 8 setup (text: 'Calculations based on N=10^4'). Three stages: no control; first mover; both control.

key_findings.finding: Nash starting times depend on degree exponent. For budget advantage, the advantaged controller starts at time 0 when lambda > 2.2; below 2.2 it starts later. Advantaged controller's per-node allocation is also larger, so the second mover can only offset, not overtake.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 9(a) lambda from 1.6 to 5 at b_A/b_B in {0.1, 1, 10}; jump in optimal start near lambda about 2.2. Fig. 9(b) per-node resource axis 1-3.5 over budget ratio 0.2-8. N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, averaged over 10 realizations, T=16.

key_findings.finding: Analytical single-node result: with fully flexible control against a constant opponent, the optimal start time satisfies a transcendental equation; a larger budget ratio pushes the start earlier.
key_findings.numbers: Equation: exp((T-t0)/2) - (T-t0)/2 = b_A/(2b) + 1 (as printed in the text, Eq. 30).

limitations: Binary opinions and simple contagion only; complex contagion and multi-state opinion models are not studied (p.22).
Assumes complete knowledge of network topology and of the opponent's strategy; partial visibility and uncertain opponent behaviour are flagged as future work (p.22-23).

Mean-field analysis assumes degree-uncorrelated networks (p.9); its accuracy is validated only on configuration-model networks and not on the five real datasets (no mean-field check reported for Table 2).
Taylor expansion valid only when (a_k+b_k)/k is small (p.10).
Individual optimization restricted to N=10^2 for computational reasons; absolute improvements described as very small (p.17-18).

Stochastic hill climbing and the iterative Nash algorithm are numerical heuristics; the text reports no optimality guarantee (p.7-8). Nash equilibria are approximated, not solved in closed form (p.8).
Individual optimization is not analysed in the game-theoretic setting because gains are small (p.22).
Integer k_min forces realized mean degree to deviate from target (target 10 gives 10.5) (p.25).
Degree exponent lower bound 1.6 chosen because lower values fail the k_min constraint (p.25).

Real datasets are not election outcome or lobbying data: Congress votes are mentions/support-oppose edges, Wikipedia Elections are user-to-user votes, Facebook and Twitter are social graphs. No validation against observed vote shares is reported.
Time horizons are abstract model units; no calendar mapping is given beyond the illustrative 30-day example (p.5).

short_quotes.quote: the best strategy for the active controller is to delay its influence
resource-rich controllers tend to start campaigns early, while resource-limited controllers strategically delay to counter their opponent's advantage
networks with more heterogeneity have longer timescales to reach equilibrium

measures: Vote share S_A(T): fraction of nodes holding opinion A at time T (Eq. 2, p.4).
Node opinion probability x_i(t) and degree-class x_k(t) (Eq. 1, 10).
Normalized order parameter r_k(t) and mean relaxation times tau_relax,k and tau_relax (Eq. 12-14, p.10-11).
Degree of equilibrium l = |S_A(T)-S_A(0)| / |S_A(inf)-S_A(0)| and l-percentage relaxation time tau^l (Eq. 19, p.13).
Degree exponent lambda and mean degree <k> (Table 1, p.11).
Relative vote share S_indiv(T)/S_const(T) for individual versus uniform optimization (Fig. 6a, 11c).
Payoffs in game: u_A = S_A(T), u_B = 1 - S_A(T) (p.7).

Cai, Brede, Gerding 2020, 'Influence maximization for dynamic allocation in voter dynamics', COMPLEX NETWORKS 2020 [12]: authors' earlier conference version; this paper adds agent heterogeneity and the game setting (p.3, p.22).
Masuda 2015, 'Opinion control in complex networks', New J. Physics [39]: source of the mean-field rate-equation framework used (p.4).

Moreno, Manino, Tran-Thanh, Brede 2020, 'Zealotry and influence maximization in the voter model: When to target partial zealots?' [41]: partial zealotry model and degree-dependent allocation pattern compared in Sec 4.3.3 (p.19).

rel.summary_md:
Cai, Gerding and Brede study a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign in a non-progressive voter model, where opinions can flip back. They use heterogeneous mean-field theory, relaxation-time analysis, hill climbing and an iterative minimax search for Nash start times. Every result is a simulation on configuration-model scale-free graphs or on five public graphs. The paper uses no observed votes, lobbying or money data.

Findings. Against a fixed opponent, the best strategy is to hold budget back and spend it late. Across all datasets, horizons and budget ratios in Table 2, an optimized start beat starting at t=0. One example is the 'Congress votes' mentions graph at T=16 with equal budgets: vote share 0.705 against 0.500. A richer controller starts earlier: on that graph the optimal start falls from 14.73 at budget ratio 0.1 to 10.48 at ratio 10. High-degree nodes take longer to settle, so on a short horizon the outcome stays far from equilibrium (degree of equilibrium never above 0.82 at T=16). In the two-controller game the side with more budget moves first, and the second mover can only offset its lead, not overtake it. Small budgets go to low-degree nodes. Partial zealots get fewer resources than normal agents.

Why it matters here. Melange's money engines have no time dimension at all. The flip model's pflip = a/(a+b) is a stationary share ratio with no time term, the optimizer allocates dollars with no timing, and the competitive cascades let a member who has been reached stay that colour. The paper is the clearest formal case in the vault that timing and reversibility change who wins under a fixed budget. Its evidence is abstract: model time units, unit edge weights, full knowledge of the network, and no calibration to any real campaign. Read it as a design critique and a source of hypotheses. It does not validate or refute any Melange constant, and any agent analysis built on it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Vote share at a finite horizon depends on when each controller starts and on degree heterogeneity. At T=16 the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82, and high-degree nodes relax more slowly. An optimized start beats t_a=0 in every real network and setting tested (Congress votes, T=16, b_A/b_B=1: S_A 0.705 vs 0.500).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2 Fig. 2-4 p.11-16; Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a and b add a saturating money pull to a peer-proximity share. It is a static, time-free share, structurally like a two-controller stationary opinion probability. Winnability is sum tgt x pflip, with no horizon, no start time and no relaxation lag.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The structural parallel holds: both are ratios of competing pulls. The magnitudes do not transfer. Paper time is dimensionless, edges have unit weight, and opinions are binary simple contagion. Nothing maps model time onto a Congress or an FEC cycle. The paper shows that an equilibrium-share model leaves out timing, not that pflip is miscalibrated.

bearings.paper_claim: Holding the budget fixed, choosing a start time (and, for N=100, a start time per node) raises final vote share over spending from t=0. A resource-limited controller should delay and spend heavily near the deadline; a resource-rich one starts early. Per-node optimization adds only small absolute gains (Fig. 6a relative axis 1.00-1.25).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 1 p.3; Sec 4.3.1-4.3.2 Fig. 5-6 p.16-18; Appendix A Eq. 30
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy places a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks with a $10k per-candidate cap (PMAX). It chooses amount per member only, never when to spend within the cycle. The objective is time-free winnability.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only as a hypothesis. PAC dollars cannot be withdrawn, FEC per-cycle limits bind, and the paper's continuous gain a_i(t) has no clear counterpart in lump-sum contributions. The finding that per-node timing adds little absolute gain suggests a single campaign start time is the extension worth building first, if any. Untested on legislators.

bearings.paper_claim: In the game, the outcome depends on the budget ratio through timing as well as level. On Congress votes at T=16 the optimal start moves from 14.73 (b_A/b_B=0.1) to 10.48 (ratio 10), and the disadvantaged second mover can only offset the leader, not overtake it (Fig. 9b per-node resource axis 1-3.5).
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head panel solves a(CU)/(a(CU)+b(comp)) = baseline odds in closed form. It reports 'CU money alone can't fully offset' when q >= 1. The solve uses the CU-to-competitor money ratio at one instant, with no sequencing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's conclusion that a disadvantaged controller can offset but not overtake agrees in spirit with the 'cannot offset' message. Its other claim, that a disadvantaged side does better by timing (delaying), has no counterpart in a static break-even. Transfer needs a model of within-cycle spending order, which the system does not have. Simulation-only evidence.

bearings.paper_claim: Competitive influence is analysed in a non-progressive model: opinions are reversible, and the opponent is a strategic controller choosing its own start time (Nash equilibrium). The second mover concentrates its budget in the final stage to pull vote share back.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 2.3 Eq. 9, Algorithm 2 p.7-8; Sec 4.3.4 Fig. 8 p.19-20
bearings.system_side: A two-colour first-to-reach independent cascade: a reached member keeps its colour for the rest of the run. Industry money enters only as non-strategic bystander activation, min(0.9, ind/400000). Nothing represents an opponent that responds in time.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a difference in model class, not evidence that the IC choice is wrong. Cosponsorship is close to progressive: withdrawals are rare. Stance and votes are not. The paper's late-countermove result matters only if the system models stance, not cosponsor joins, as the contested state.

bearings.paper_claim: With 20% partial zealots, normal agents receive more resources than zealots at every zealotry level q. At medium and large q, zealots get fewer resources and later starts as degree rises (lowest q=0.1: maximum zealot allocation under 20 vs about 25 for normal agents).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.3.3 Fig. 7 p.19-20; Appendix E Fig. 11 p.26-27
bearings.system_side: PERS gives committed or resistant tiers a low target multiplier: Opponent 0.08, Highly Skeptical 0.15, Champion 0.10. Middle tiers sit around 0.50-0.65. The F1 gate gives Skeptic, Highly Skeptical and Opponent members zero money.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The direction agrees: resistant agents get less. The paper never allocates zero to zealots at low q, so it does not support a hard zero gate on its own. Its zealotry is one-sided resistance to adopting A, which maps loosely onto Skeptic and Opponent and not onto Champion. Simulated agents only.

bearings.paper_claim: Under node-specific optimization, the budget ratio sets the degree pattern. With small budgets, control gains fall and start times rise with degree, so low-degree nodes are targeted. With large budgets the pattern reverses.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.3.2 Fig. 6(b)-(c) p.18; Appendix D Fig. 10 p.26
bearings.system_side: The coalition water-fill boosts candidates by (1 + 0.8 bpf), favouring bipartisan bridges, and ranks them by marginal spread. Budget size never changes which structural position is preferred.
bearings.transfer_conditions: bpf is a cross-party share, not degree, so the paper's degree result maps only indirectly. The paper's result rests on N=100 graphs with mean degree 6. Measuring the Melange cosponsor graph's degree exponent, and testing whether the seeds chosen by greedy spread move toward low-degree members at small budgets, would be new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED.

gaps_exposed: No time dimension in any money or influence engine. optimize.py, flip_model.py, budget_frontier.py and scenario.py allocate amounts with no start time, horizon or spending schedule, although the paper shows timing alone shifts final share under a fixed budget.

No model of a strategic opponent. Competitor money is a fixed input or bystander noise (min(0.9, ind/400000)), never a best-responding player, so the system cannot represent a late countermove by banks.

No reversibility. Competitive cascades are first-to-reach and absorbing, while stance in the paper (and in reality) can revert. stance_dynamics measures trajectories, but the allocators do not consume them.
The degree heterogeneity (degree exponent) of the cosponsor graph is unmeasured, though the paper makes optimal timing and degree targeting depend on it, with a regime change near lambda 2.2.

The contested-bills registry has a schema for a counterparty but no consumer, so the paper's two-controller game framing has nowhere to land (fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py:1-20 says no consumer exists).
flags: The paper's 'Congress votes' dataset is a network of mentions between politicians with support/oppose edges. It is not roll calls or cosponsorship, and Table 2 'vote share' is model output, not observed votes. Never quote 0.705 vs 0.500 as an electoral or legislative effect.
'Influence' in the paper is a model-internal controller gain. Under D-025, no bearing here may be read as closeness, access or a probability of moving a member.
Every number in the paper is in dimensionless model time on unit-weight graphs. Any figure carried over must name that window and denominator (N, mean degree, lambda, T, realizations).
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization; it uses unit weights as a simplification. Neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated.
A degree-exponent measurement or timing test on Melange graphs would be new agent analysis. It stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The component list says contested-bills cites Romero Moreno 2021, but fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py contains no such citation. The link lives only in notes.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It speaks most directly to two of his positions. On competitive-cascade-crn, he wants rival industries modelled and scenarios simulated cheaply. The paper supports the first and goes further: a rival should be a strategic, time-aware player, which the system does not have. On joint-optimizer, he sees adaptive greedy plus CELF as the operational layer and expects learned policies to replace it at scale. The paper adds a missing axis, when to spend, that neither greedy nor GCOMB covers as built. His Kim J. 2025 margin note about conflicting industries is consistent with the two-controller game. His notes are not stale here; the system simply has no timing layer for them to describe. His ROI enthusiasm should be tempered by the paper's own result that per-node fine-tuning yields very small absolute gains.

related.why: Same Brede group and voter-model continuous IM framework. The paper compares its zealotry allocation pattern with this line of work (Moreno et al.), and the contested-bills component is linked to Romero Moreno 2021.

Bharathi's progressive competitive IC is the model class behind competitive-cascade-crn. Cai uses a non-progressive, reversible voter model with a strategic opponent, an alternative formalization with different optimal behavior.
Borodin's competitive threshold models (cited in flip_model for lacking submodularity) and Cai's timing game both show that competition breaks simple greedy guarantees.
Golovin-Krause supports the optimizer's static greedy bound. Cai adds a temporal allocation dimension that the bound does not cover.
Chen's contingency-aware seeding (SGATE) and Cai's partial zealotry both model agents who resist adoption. Cai finds such agents receive fewer resources.
Salience-shock timing (going public) is the empirical analogue of a controller's start-time choice, which Cai studies only abstractly.
